vignette: It begins on a damp March evening, three years ago. He walks home from a late client dinner, a manila folder of receipts tucked under his arm. The streetlights on his block are out. Two patrol cars roll slowly past, blue lights slicing through the fog. Before he can reach his key, a command cuts through the air. His hands rise on their own. He hears boots, the heavy clack of a baton against a thigh, the metallic snap of cuffs before his wrists even touch his belt. He does not resist. He counts his breaths against the cold pavement, the weight of a knee pressing into his spine, until the siren fades and he is left bleeding in a puddle of spilled receipts. He never learns the official reason for the stop. He only remembers the absolute, terrifying certainty that his body has been commandeered. In the months that follow, the numbers he once trusted begin to fracture. At his desk, he reconstructs quarterly projections for mid-sized Latin American import businesses, but his focus splinters. He finds himself avoiding client calls after five p.m., his stomach knotting at the vibration of his phone. When a client arrives for a consultation wearing a navy blazer, Carlos feels his shoulders lock, his throat constricting around words he cannot force out. He starts double-checking every deduction, every signature, convinced that one misplaced decimal will trigger an investigation that ends exactly like that night. He takes detours that add forty minutes to his commute, steering clear of parks, train stations, and any street where uniformed officers gather. His marriage ended six months before the incident, and the divorce papers now sit in a drawer next to the kitchen knife he keeps under his pillow. He tells me that sleeping used to be simple, but now it requires a checklist: deadbolt engaged twice, windows latched, phone face-down, hallway clear. He wakes at 3 a.m. most nights, heart hammering, convinced he hears the rhythm of boots in the hallway. When his daughter visits, he cooks for her, but he sits with his back to the wall, eyes tracking the door. He says he feels like a ghost in his own life, watching himself move through routines that no longer feel entirely his. Now, in the quiet of this room, he unclenches his jaw. The pen stops tapping. He tells me that the world feels thinner, more brittle, and that he carries a quiet, constant exhaustion, as if his nervous system has been running a marathon for years without a finish line. He still goes to work. He still files returns. But he waits for the other shoe to drop, his hands steady on the desk, his gaze distant, his breath measured. He is here. He is still trying to remember how to land.
